blocks.text: SOCIOLOGY
SEMESTER V & VI
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

Rural Sociology is the branch of sociology concerned with rural society, rural institutions, relationships and social change. Its development is connected with the systematic study of village life, agrarian relations and rural transformation.

Rural Sociology developed first in the United States in the early twentieth century, when rapid industrialization and migration drew attention to the problems of farm communities. The Country Life Commission appointed by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 and the work of scholars such as C.J. Galpin, Pitirim Sorokin and Carle C. Zimmerman helped establish the field. Sorokin and Zimmerman's 'Principles of Rural-Urban Sociology' (1929) was an important early text.

In India, rural sociology grew after independence because most Indians lived in villages and planned development focused on rural areas. Village studies by M.N. Srinivas, S.C. Dube, McKim Marriott, F.G. Bailey and Andre Beteille, and A.R. Desai's 'Rural Sociology in India', shaped the discipline.

A.R. Desai stressed that, since India is mainly a rural country, rural sociology is necessary for understanding Indian society and for planning its development. Census 2011 recorded about 68.8 per cent of India's population as rural.

sections.title: Nature and Scope of Rural Sociology

blocks.text: Its scope includes rural social structure, caste and class, family and community, agriculture, rural institutions, rural-urban relations, social change and rural development.

Rural Sociology is a scientific, empirical and applied discipline. It studies rural society systematically and also aims to help rural reconstruction and development. Its nature is both descriptive (what rural society is like) and analytical (why and how it changes).

Its scope covers rural social organization (family, kinship, caste, class), rural institutions (panchayat, religion, education), the rural economy (agriculture, land tenure, cooperatives, markets), rural problems (poverty, indebtedness, unemployment, illiteracy, health), rural leadership and politics, rural-urban relations and migration, and rural development programmes and their evaluation.

The importance of rural sociology lies in understanding village life, guiding policy, evaluating development programmes, promoting participation of rural people and helping to reduce rural-urban inequality.

Rural and urban societies differ in occupation, population density, social relations and institutions, but they are not completely separate. The rural-urban continuum emphasizes gradual differences and increasing interaction between villages and towns.

Sorokin and Zimmerman listed differences between rural and urban communities on the basis of occupation (agriculture versus industry and services), environment (closeness to nature versus a man-made environment), size of community (small versus large), density of population (low versus high), homogeneity (rural areas more homogeneous), social differentiation and stratification (simpler versus more complex), mobility (less versus more) and systems of interaction (personal versus impersonal).

Robert Redfield's concept of the 'folk-urban continuum', developed from his studies in Mexico, suggested that communities can be placed along a line from small, isolated, homogeneous folk societies to large, heterogeneous urban societies. The 'rural-urban continuum' similarly holds that there is no sharp break between village and city.

In India, urban influences reach villages through roads, mobile phones, television, markets and migration, while cities contain migrants who keep rural ties. Census 2011 also identified 'census towns' — settlements with urban characteristics still governed as villages — showing the blurred boundary between rural and urban.
Rural stratification in India historically connected caste position with land, occupation and class. These relations varied locally but often shaped access to resources and social status.

In traditional Indian villages, upper castes generally owned land, middle castes were often cultivators or artisans, and lower castes, including Dalits, were mostly landless labourers or service providers. Caste and class therefore overlapped, a situation sometimes described as 'caste-class nexus'.

Andre Beteille's study of Sripuram in Tamil Nadu ('Caste, Class and Power', 1965) showed that Brahmins once dominated land ownership, ritual status and political power, but that these dimensions were becoming separated as non-Brahmins gained land and political influence.

The jajmani system linked landowning patrons with service castes through hereditary ties, reinforcing the caste-class nexus. Srinivas's concept of the 'dominant caste' explains how a caste that is numerically strong and controls land can dominate village affairs even without the highest ritual rank.

Commercial agriculture, land reforms, markets, technology and new employment contributed to the emergence of differentiated rural classes such as large farmers, middle peasants, small cultivators and agricultural labourers.

Daniel Thorner classified agrarian classes as maliks (landlords), kisans (working peasants) and mazdurs (labourers). Other scholars distinguish rich farmers, middle peasants, small and marginal farmers, tenants, sharecroppers and landless agricultural labourers.

Factors that created new rural classes include the colonial land revenue systems (zamindari, ryotwari and mahalwari), commercialization of agriculture, abolition of zamindari after independence, land ceiling laws, the Green Revolution and access to credit and markets.

The Green Revolution produced a class of prosperous 'capitalist farmers' in regions such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, who became politically influential, while small farmers and labourers often remained poor. Utsa Patnaik and others debated whether Indian agriculture was moving towards capitalism.

Education, democracy, migration, occupational mobility and economic change have altered caste relations in rural society, although caste continues to influence marriage, identity and local social relations.

Changes in rural caste include the decline of untouchability practices in public places, weakening of the jajmani system, occupational diversification, reservation in panchayats under the 73rd Amendment (1992), and rising political assertion of backward castes and Dalits.

M.N. Srinivas noted that caste has become more important as a basis of political mobilization even as its ritual aspects weaken. Rural Dalits have gained education and political representation, but caste-based violence and discrimination still occur in some areas.

In tribal states such as Mizoram, caste is largely absent from village social structure. Stratification there has been based more on clan, chieftainship (until its abolition in 1954), wealth and education.

sections.title: Functions of Caste in Rural Society

blocks.text: Caste historically organized occupations, marriage relations, status, social networks and local cooperation. Modern social change has weakened many traditional functions.

Caste performed several functions in traditional rural society: it fixed occupations and provided a division of labour; it regulated marriage through endogamy; it provided social security and mutual help within the caste; it acted as an agency of social control through caste panchayats; and it gave members an identity and a sense of belonging.
Caste also had serious dysfunctions: it created inequality, untouchability and exploitation, restricted mobility, and divided rural society.
With modernization, many traditional functions have been taken over by the state, the market, schools and panchayats, but caste associations continue to function as interest groups.
Technology, education, migration, markets, democratic politics, communication, state programmes and changing aspirations are major forces transforming rural society.

Forces of change include the Green Revolution and agricultural technology (tractors, high-yielding seeds, fertilizers, irrigation), land reforms, Panchayati Raj, community development programmes (started in 1952), cooperative movements, rural electrification, roads under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (2000), mobile phones and the internet, and migration.

Education and the media spread new ideas about equality, health and rights. Government schemes for housing, sanitation (Swachh Bharat Mission - Gramin, 2014) and drinking water (Jal Jeevan Mission, 2019) have changed living conditions.

In Mizoram, the shift from jhum (shifting cultivation) to settled farming and horticulture, supported by programmes such as the New Land Use Policy, and the spread of education and government employment have transformed village life.
Voluntary organizations, community groups and other civil-society bodies can support participation, awareness, accountability and local development.

Civil society refers to the space of voluntary associations between the family and the state, including NGOs, self-help groups, cooperatives, farmers' organizations, religious bodies, community-based organizations and social movements.

In rural development, civil society helps by creating awareness, mobilizing people, delivering services such as health and education, monitoring government programmes through social audits, protecting rights and representing the voices of the poor.

Examples include the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA), the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS), whose campaign helped lead to the Right to Information Act, 2005, and Amul in the dairy cooperative movement. In Mizoram, the YMA, MHIP and church organizations play an important role in village welfare.
Contemporary rural society shows diversification of occupations, greater mobility, expanding education, stronger market connections and closer rural-urban interaction.

Rural India today is no longer only agricultural. A large share of rural household income comes from non-farm work such as construction, trade, transport and services. Many rural households depend on remittances from migrant members.

Other features of the emerging rural society include the spread of education and mobile phones, the growth of self-help groups led by women, increased participation of women and marginalized groups in panchayats, and greater consumer aspirations.
Challenges remain, including agrarian distress, small landholdings, indebtedness, farmer suicides, water scarcity, climate change and gaps in health and education services.
MGNREGS is a rural employment programme designed to provide wage employment through public works and strengthen livelihood security in rural areas.

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. The scheme under the Act is MGNREGS.

Important features include a legal right to work; employment within 5 km of residence where possible; payment of an unemployment allowance if work is not provided within 15 days; at least one-third of beneficiaries to be women; works such as water conservation, land development and rural roads; social audits by the Gram Sabha; and payment of wages into bank or post office accounts.

MGNREGS has helped reduce distress migration, increased rural wages and women's income, and created rural assets. Criticisms include delays in wage payments, corruption in some areas and poor quality of some assets.
The National Rural Livelihoods Mission promotes rural livelihoods, especially through self-help groups, access to credit, skills and collective organization.

The National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM) was launched in 2011 by the Ministry of Rural Development, replacing the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY). It was renamed Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) in 2015-16. It is known as 'Aajeevika'.

The mission aims to bring at least one woman from each poor rural household into self-help groups (SHGs), federate them at village and higher levels, and provide access to bank credit, financial services, skill training and livelihood support.

Sub-components include the Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana (for women farmers) and the Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme. In Mizoram, the State Rural Livelihoods Mission implements NRLM through SHGs in villages.
The Integrated Rural Development Programme was designed to assist poor rural households through productive assets, credit and income-generating activities.

The Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) was introduced on a pilot basis in 1978-79 and extended to all blocks of the country from 2 October 1980. It aimed to help families below the poverty line cross the poverty line by providing productive assets and inputs through subsidies and bank credit.

Target groups included small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, rural artisans and SC/ST households, with special attention to women. Assets included milch animals, small business, and tools for artisans.

Evaluations found problems such as wrong selection of beneficiaries, inadequate credit, poor follow-up, corruption and assets not suited to local conditions. In 1999, IRDP and several related programmes were merged into the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), which was later replaced by NRLM.
The syllabus lists PMRHS among rural development programmes. Students should retain the programme name as given in the prescribed syllabus.

Students should check with their teacher or the latest syllabus for the exact full form of 'PMRHS' as intended in this course, since abbreviations of rural schemes can be confused. Rural housing in India is currently provided under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G), launched in 2016 as a restructuring of the Indira Awaas Yojana (1985).

The Ministry of Rural Development also ran the Prime Minister's Rural Development Fellows Scheme (PMRDFS) from 2011, which placed young professionals in districts affected by left-wing extremism to assist district administrations. When writing about any rural development programme, students should state its aim, year of launch, target group, main features, achievements and limitations.

Rural Sociology: Rural Sociology is the branch of sociology concerned with rural society, rural institutions, relationships and social change. Its development is connected with the systematic study of village life, agrarian relations and rural transformation. Nature and Scope of Rural Sociology: Its scope includes rural social structure, caste and class, family and community, agriculture, rural institutions, rural-urban relations, social change and rural development. Rural–Urban Differences and Continuum: Rural and urban societies differ in occupation, population density, social relations and institutions, but they are not completely separate. Traditional Caste and Class Nexus: Rural stratification in India historically connected caste position with land, occupation and class. These relations varied locally but often shaped access to resources and social status.

Rural Sociology as a discipline studies the social life of rural people scientifically. In the United States it developed in response to rural problems in the early twentieth century, and in India it gained importance after independence with community development and village studies. Its subject matter includes the village community, family, caste, class, religion, economy, politics and change.

Rural and urban societies differ in occupation, size, density, homogeneity, mobility, social interaction and stratification, as Sorokin and Zimmerman explained. However, Redfield's folk-urban continuum and the rural-urban continuum approach show that these differences are of degree, not of kind, and that villages and cities are increasingly interconnected.

The traditional rural social structure in India was based on the overlap of caste and class, with upper castes controlling land and lower castes providing labour and services. Studies by Beteille, Srinivas and others showed how land ownership, ritual status and political power were linked in villages, and how these links began to loosen after independence.
In conclusion, students should define rural sociology, explain its nature and scope, compare rural and urban society using the continuum approach, and discuss the caste-class nexus with examples.

Changing Rural Caste Stratification: Education, democracy, migration, occupational mobility and economic change have altered caste relations in rural society, although caste continues to influence marriage, identity and local social relations. Modern social change has weakened many traditional functions. Forces of Rural Social Change: Technology, education, migration, markets, democratic politics, communication, state programmes and changing aspirations are major forces transforming rural society.

Rural class stratification emerged through colonial land policies, the commercialization of agriculture, land reforms and the Green Revolution. Rural society today is divided into rich farmers, middle peasants, small and marginal farmers, tenants and agricultural labourers, though caste and class still overlap in many areas.

Caste in rural society has changed through education, Panchayati Raj, reservation, migration and occupational diversification. Untouchability and the jajmani system have declined, but caste continues in marriage, identity, politics and sometimes conflict.

Caste performed functions of division of labour, social security, marriage regulation and social control, but also caused inequality and exploitation. Many of its functions have been taken over by modern institutions.

Forces of rural change include technology, the Green Revolution, land reforms, education, the media, migration, community development, Panchayati Raj and government schemes. Together they have produced a more diversified and connected rural society, though rural inequality and distress remain.

Civil Society in Rural Development: Voluntary organizations, community groups and other civil-society bodies can support participation, awareness, accountability and local development. Emerging Rural Society in India: Contemporary rural society shows diversification of occupations, greater mobility, expanding education, stronger market connections and closer rural-urban interaction. MGNREGS: MGNREGS is a rural employment programme designed to provide wage employment through public works and strengthen livelihood security in rural areas. NRLM: The National Rural Livelihoods Mission promotes rural livelihoods, especially through self-help groups, access to credit, skills and collective organization.

Civil society organizations play a key role in rural development by mobilizing people, delivering services, building self-help groups and ensuring accountability through social audits and campaigns such as the right to information movement.

The emerging rural society in India is characterized by non-farm employment, migration, education, communication technology, women's participation through SHGs and panchayats, and closer links with urban markets.

MGNREGS (2005) provides a legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment, creates rural assets, empowers women and reduces distress migration. NRLM (2011), now DAY-NRLM, organizes poor rural women into SHGs and links them with credit and livelihoods.
In conclusion, rural development in India has moved from top-down programmes towards rights-based and participatory approaches in which the rural poor, especially women, are active participants.

IRDP: The Integrated Rural Development Programme was designed to assist poor rural households through productive assets, credit and income-generating activities. PMRHS: The syllabus lists PMRHS among rural development programmes. Students should retain the programme name as given in the prescribed syllabus.

IRDP (1978-80) was a major self-employment programme that provided subsidized assets and credit to poor rural families. It was criticized for poor targeting and leakage, and was merged into SGSY in 1999, which was later replaced by NRLM.

Rural housing has been addressed through the Indira Awaas Yojana (1985) and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Gramin (2016), which provides financial assistance to houseless and kutcha-house households to build pucca houses with basic amenities. Students should confirm the exact scheme intended by 'PMRHS' in their syllabus.

When evaluating rural development programmes, sociologists examine whether benefits reach the poorest, the role of local institutions, women's participation, corruption, sustainability of assets and the impact on social relations in the village.
Overall, rural development programmes have reduced poverty and improved infrastructure, but challenges of implementation, inequality and agrarian distress continue.

SHORT NOTES
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

sections.title: Auguste Comte: Law of Three Stages
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Comte argued that human thought passes through theological, metaphysical and positive stages. In the positive stage, explanation is based on observation and scientific reasoning.

Comte (1798-1857) explained the Law of Three Stages in his 'Course of Positive Philosophy' (1830-1842). In the theological stage, people explain events as the actions of supernatural beings; this stage passes through fetishism, polytheism and monotheism. In the metaphysical stage, explanations are based on abstract forces or essences, such as 'nature'. In the positive stage, explanations are based on observation, experiment and scientific laws.

Comte linked each stage to a form of social organization: the theological stage to military society ruled by priests and warriors; the metaphysical stage to a transitional legalistic society; and the positive stage to industrial society guided by scientists and industrialists.
Critics argue that the stages are speculative and that different types of thinking can exist at the same time in one society.

sections.title: Social Statics and Social Dynamics
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Social statics concerns the conditions of social order and stability, while social dynamics concerns social progress and change. Comte used both to explain society as an ordered yet developing system.

Comte compared social statics to anatomy, which studies the structure of the body, and social dynamics to physiology, which studies its functioning and development. Statics studies the 'laws of coexistence' and the conditions of social order, such as the family, religion, language and division of labour.
Social dynamics studies the 'laws of succession', or how society progresses through stages. For Comte, order and progress were complementary: progress must take place within order.
This distinction influenced later functionalist and evolutionary theories in sociology.

sections.title: Positivism
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Positivism holds that society should be studied through systematic observation and scientific methods rather than speculation alone. Comte regarded Sociology as a positive science.

Comte believed that society, like nature, is governed by invariable laws that can be discovered through observation, comparison, experiment and the historical method. He called this approach 'positivism'.

Durkheim continued the positivist tradition by treating social facts as things and using statistics to study suicide. Later, positivism was criticized by interpretive sociologists such as Weber, who argued that understanding human meaning requires methods different from the natural sciences.
Comte also proposed a 'Religion of Humanity' in his later work, in which humanity itself would be worshipped and sociologists would act as priests, an idea widely criticized.

sections.title: Classification of Sciences
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Comte arranged sciences in an order from simpler and more general sciences toward more complex ones, placing Sociology at the highest level because it studies complex social phenomena.
Comte's hierarchy of sciences was: mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology and sociology. Each science depends on those before it and is more complex and less general.
Sociology is at the top because it is the most complex science and depends on all the others. Comte called it the 'queen of sciences'.
Psychology was not included as a separate science in his classification; he treated it partly under biology and partly under sociology.

sections.title: Marx: Historical Materialism
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Historical materialism explains social development through material conditions and modes of production. Changes in productive forces and relations of production create contradictions that contribute to historical transformation.

Karl Marx (1818-1883), a German thinker, developed historical materialism with Friedrich Engels. In the preface to 'A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy' (1859), Marx wrote that 'it is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but, on the contrary, their social being that determines their consciousness'.

Marx distinguished between the economic base (forces of production such as tools, technology and labour, and relations of production such as ownership) and the superstructure (law, politics, religion, family, art and ideas). Changes in the base lead to changes in the superstructure.

Marx identified stages of history based on modes of production: primitive communism, ancient (slave) society, feudalism, capitalism and, in the future, socialism and communism. He also discussed an 'Asiatic mode of production' for certain Asian societies.

sections.title: Theory of Social Class
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: For Marx, class is closely related to a group's position in the system of production. Under capitalism, the major opposition is between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who sell labour.

Marx defined class by the relationship to the means of production. In capitalism, the bourgeoisie own factories, land and capital, while the proletariat own only their labour power, which they sell for wages. Marx also mentioned intermediate classes such as the petty bourgeoisie, which he expected to decline.

He distinguished 'class in itself' (a group sharing the same economic position) from 'class for itself' (a class conscious of its common interests and organized to struggle). False consciousness occurs when workers accept the ideas of the ruling class.
Marx's theory of surplus value explained exploitation: workers produce more value than they receive as wages, and the surplus is taken by capitalists as profit.

sections.title: Class Struggle
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Marx viewed conflict between classes with opposed material interests as a major force of historical change.

'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' is the opening line of 'The Communist Manifesto' (1848) by Marx and Engels. Examples include freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, and bourgeoisie and proletariat.
Marx predicted that capitalism would create crises, increase the misery of workers (pauperization) and polarize society into two classes, leading to a proletarian revolution and a classless society.
Critics note that the revolution did not occur in advanced capitalist countries as predicted, the middle class expanded, and welfare states reduced class conflict.

sections.title: Alienation
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Alienation describes the worker's separation from the product of labour, the labour process, other people and human creative potential under capitalist conditions.

Marx discussed alienation in the 'Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844'. He described four forms: alienation from the product of labour (which belongs to the capitalist), alienation from the process of labour (work becomes forced and meaningless), alienation from species-being (human creative nature), and alienation from other human beings (relations become competitive and money-based).
Alienation results from private property and the division of labour under capitalism. Marx believed it would end only in a communist society where workers control production.
Later sociologists, such as Robert Blauner in 'Alienation and Freedom' (1964), studied alienation empirically in different industries.

sections.title: Durkheim: Social Facts
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Social facts are ways of acting, thinking and feeling that exist outside individuals and exercise constraint over them. Durkheim argued that they should be studied as social realities.

Emile Durkheim (1858-1917) explained social facts in 'The Rules of Sociological Method' (1895). Social facts have two characteristics: externality (they exist outside the individual) and constraint (they exert pressure on the individual). Examples include law, language, religious beliefs, customs and the monetary system.

Durkheim's first rule was to 'consider social facts as things', meaning they should be studied objectively, without preconceptions. He also said social facts should be explained by other social facts, not by individual psychology.
He distinguished normal social facts (found generally in a society) from pathological ones (abnormal or exceptional).

sections.title: Theory of Suicide
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Durkheim explained variations in suicide rates sociologically through levels of social integration and regulation, showing that apparently individual acts can have social causes.

In 'Suicide' (1897), Durkheim used statistics from several European countries to show that suicide rates vary with social conditions. He identified four types: egoistic suicide (too little integration, such as among isolated individuals or Protestants compared to Catholics), altruistic suicide (too much integration, such as soldiers sacrificing themselves or sati), anomic suicide (too little regulation, during economic crises or sudden changes) and fatalistic suicide (too much regulation, such as among slaves).

Durkheim found that suicide rates were lower among Catholics than Protestants, lower among married people than the unmarried, and lower during times of war or national crisis because of stronger integration.
Critics, such as J.D. Douglas, argued that official suicide statistics are socially constructed and may be unreliable. Nevertheless, Durkheim's study is a classic example of the sociological method.

sections.title: Crime and Deviance
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Durkheim treated crime as a normal social phenomenon because all societies define certain acts as violations. Responses to deviance can reinforce collective norms.

In 'The Rules of Sociological Method', Durkheim argued that crime is normal because it is found in all societies. A society without crime is impossible because people will always differ from collective norms.

Crime has positive functions: punishment reaffirms collective values and strengthens solidarity, and crime can sometimes lead to social change, as when a person punished for challenging norms is later seen as a reformer (Durkheim gave the example of Socrates).
However, Durkheim considered too much crime pathological, a sign of social disorganization or anomie.

sections.title: Division of Labour
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Durkheim connected increasing division of labour with a movement from mechanical solidarity toward organic solidarity based on interdependence.

In 'The Division of Labour in Society' (1893), Durkheim distinguished mechanical solidarity, found in simple societies where people are similar and share a strong collective conscience, from organic solidarity, found in complex societies where people are different but depend on each other due to specialization.
Mechanical solidarity is reflected in repressive law (punishment), while organic solidarity is reflected in restitutive law (restoring relations, such as contract and civil law).

He identified abnormal forms of the division of labour: the anomic division of labour (lack of regulation), the forced division of labour (when people are forced into roles that do not match their abilities) and poor coordination.

sections.title: Weber: Social Action
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Social action is action to which an individual attaches meaning and which is oriented toward others. Weber made interpretive understanding of meaningful action central to sociology.

Max Weber (1864-1920) defined sociology as 'a science concerning itself with the interpretive understanding of social action'. He used the method of 'Verstehen' (understanding), which means grasping the meaning that actors attach to their actions.

Weber identified four types of social action: zweckrational or instrumentally rational action (choosing efficient means for an end, such as an engineer building a bridge), wertrational or value-rational action (action guided by a value regardless of consequences, such as a captain going down with the ship), affectual action (guided by emotions) and traditional action (guided by custom and habit).
Weber argued that modern society is characterized by increasing rationalization, which leads to the 'disenchantment of the world' and the growth of bureaucracy.

sections.title: Ideal Types
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: An ideal type is an analytical model that emphasizes selected characteristics of a social phenomenon. It is used as a conceptual tool for comparison rather than as a perfect description of reality.

An ideal type is a mental construct formed by exaggerating certain features of a phenomenon. It is 'ideal' not in the sense of perfect or desirable, but in the sense of being a pure form of an idea. Examples include Weber's ideal types of bureaucracy, authority and the Protestant ethic.
Ideal types help in comparison: real cases can be measured against the ideal type to see how they differ. They are not hypotheses or averages.
Weber distinguished historical ideal types (such as 'capitalism' or 'the Protestant ethic') and general ideal types (such as types of action and authority).

sections.title: Types of Authority
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Weber distinguished traditional authority, charismatic authority and legal-rational authority according to the basis on which legitimacy is accepted.

Weber defined authority as legitimate power, meaning power accepted as rightful by those over whom it is exercised. Traditional authority is based on custom and inherited status, such as a king or chief. Charismatic authority is based on the extraordinary personal qualities of a leader, such as a prophet or revolutionary leader. Legal-rational authority is based on rules and laws, such as an elected government or a bureaucrat.
Charismatic authority is unstable and tends to become 'routinized' into traditional or legal-rational authority after the leader's death.
In traditional Mizo society, chiefs exercised traditional authority; today, elected Village Councils and state institutions represent legal-rational authority.

sections.title: Bureaucracy
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Weber described bureaucracy as an organization based on hierarchy, specialization, written rules, official competence and impersonal administration.

Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy has the following features: a fixed division of labour; a hierarchy of offices; written rules and records (files); impersonality; appointment based on technical qualifications; salaried full-time officials; a career with promotion based on seniority or merit; and separation of official and private property.
Weber regarded bureaucracy as the most efficient form of organization but warned that it could become an 'iron cage' that limits human freedom.
Critics, such as Robert Merton, pointed out the dysfunctions of bureaucracy, including red tape, rigid adherence to rules ('trained incapacity') and goal displacement.

sections.title: Unit 1 – Comprehensive Note
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

In the positive stage, explanation is based on observation and scientific reasoning. Comte used both to explain society as an ordered yet developing system. Positivism: Positivism holds that society should be studied through systematic observation and scientific methods rather than speculation alone. Comte regarded Sociology as a positive science. Classification of Sciences: Comte arranged sciences in an order from simpler and more general sciences toward more complex ones, placing Sociology at the highest level because it studies complex social phenomena.

Auguste Comte is called the father of sociology because he coined the term and argued for a scientific study of society. His Law of Three Stages explained the development of human thought from theological to metaphysical to positive (scientific) thinking, with corresponding forms of social organization.

Comte's distinction between social statics (order) and social dynamics (progress) laid the foundation for later theories of social structure and change. His positivism argued that society should be studied by observation, experiment, comparison and historical method.
His hierarchy of sciences (mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology and sociology) placed sociology at the top as the most complex science.

Comte has been criticized for speculation, for an overly optimistic belief in progress, and for his later Religion of Humanity. Nevertheless, his ideas strongly influenced Durkheim and the development of sociology as a science.

sections.title: Unit 2 – Comprehensive Note
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Marx: Historical Materialism: Historical materialism explains social development through material conditions and modes of production. Changes in productive forces and relations of production create contradictions that contribute to historical transformation. Theory of Social Class: For Marx, class is closely related to a group's position in the system of production. Under capitalism, the major opposition is between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who sell labour. Class Struggle: Marx viewed conflict between classes with opposed material interests as a major force of historical change. Alienation: Alienation describes the worker's separation from the product of labour, the labour process, other people and human creative potential under capitalist conditions.

Marx's historical materialism holds that material production is the basis of social life and that history advances through changes in modes of production, driven by contradictions between forces and relations of production.

Marx's theory of class defines classes by their relation to the means of production. Capitalism is characterized by the conflict between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. The proletariat becomes a 'class for itself' when it develops class consciousness.

Class struggle is the engine of history, and Marx expected it to lead to a socialist revolution and eventually a classless, communist society. His concept of alienation describes how workers under capitalism are estranged from the product, the process, their human nature and other people.
Marx's ideas have been criticized for economic determinism and failed predictions, but they remain central to conflict theory and to the study of inequality, labour, globalization and ideology.

sections.title: Unit 3 – Comprehensive Note
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Durkheim: Social Facts: Social facts are ways of acting, thinking and feeling that exist outside individuals and exercise constraint over them. Durkheim argued that they should be studied as social realities. Theory of Suicide: Durkheim explained variations in suicide rates sociologically through levels of social integration and regulation, showing that apparently individual acts can have social causes. Crime and Deviance: Durkheim treated crime as a normal social phenomenon because all societies define certain acts as violations. Responses to deviance can reinforce collective norms. Division of Labour: Durkheim connected increasing division of labour with a movement from mechanical solidarity toward organic solidarity based on interdependence.

Durkheim established sociology as an independent academic discipline. His concept of social facts emphasized the external and constraining character of social phenomena and the need to study them objectively.
His study of suicide showed how social integration and regulation influence suicide rates and identified egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic suicide.

Durkheim argued that crime is normal and functional because it reaffirms collective values and can promote change. In 'The Division of Labour in Society', he explained the shift from mechanical solidarity in simple societies to organic solidarity in complex societies.
Durkheim's work laid the foundations of functionalism and influenced later sociologists such as Radcliffe-Brown, Parsons and Merton.

sections.title: Unit 4 – Comprehensive Note
context: SOC/MJ/301 – FOUNDATION OF SOCIOLOGICAL THOUGHT – I

blocks.text: Weber: Social Action: Social action is action to which an individual attaches meaning and which is oriented toward others. Weber made interpretive understanding of meaningful action central to sociology. Ideal Types: An ideal type is an analytical model that emphasizes selected characteristics of a social phenomenon. It is used as a conceptual tool for comparison rather than as a perfect description of reality. Types of Authority: Weber distinguished traditional authority, charismatic authority and legal-rational authority according to the basis on which legitimacy is accepted. Bureaucracy: Weber described bureaucracy as an organization based on hierarchy, specialization, written rules, official competence and impersonal administration.
Max Weber emphasized interpretive understanding (Verstehen) of social action and distinguished four types: instrumentally rational, value-rational, affectual and traditional.
His methodological tool, the ideal type, allows comparison of real cases with a pure conceptual model.

Weber identified three types of legitimate authority — traditional, charismatic and legal-rational — and analysed bureaucracy as the characteristic form of legal-rational authority in modern society, while warning about its 'iron cage'.

Weber's other important work includes 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' (1905) and his three-dimensional view of stratification (class, status and party). His work balances Marx's emphasis on economics by showing the importance of ideas and values.
Social stratification refers to structured inequality in which individuals and groups are ranked into unequal social positions. It affects access to wealth, power, prestige and opportunities.

Melvin Tumin defined stratification as 'the arrangement of any social group or society into a hierarchy of positions that are unequal with regard to power, property, social evaluation and psychic gratification'. Ogburn and Nimkoff described it as the process by which individuals and groups are ranked in a more or less enduring hierarchy of status.
The four main systems of stratification are slavery, estates (in feudal Europe), caste (in India) and class (in modern industrial societies).
Stratification affects 'life chances', a term used by Weber for the opportunities a person has in health, education, income and longevity.
Stratification is social, relatively persistent, hierarchical and connected with unequal rewards and life chances. Its form differs across societies.

Tumin listed the characteristics of stratification: it is social (based on social, not biological, differences); it is ancient; it is universal; it is diverse in form; and it is consequential (it affects life chances and lifestyles).
Stratification is maintained by beliefs and ideologies that justify inequality, such as the doctrine of karma in the caste system or the idea of meritocracy in class societies.
Stratification persists across generations because families pass on wealth, education and social connections to their children.
Caste is a hereditary form of stratification traditionally associated with hierarchy, endogamy, occupational links and restrictions on social relations.

Caste is a closed system of stratification in which membership is determined by birth and mobility is very limited. G.S. Ghurye identified its features as segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, restrictions on occupation and endogamy.
Louis Dumont emphasized the principle of purity and pollution as the basis of the caste hierarchy. Srinivas noted that Sanskritization allows limited group mobility within the system.
Caste-like systems have been noted in other societies, but the Indian caste system is the most elaborate example.
Class is a system of stratification based strongly on economic position and life chances. Class boundaries are generally more open than caste boundaries.
Class is an open system of stratification based mainly on economic factors such as income, wealth and occupation. Mobility is possible through education and achievement.

Marx defined class by ownership of the means of production, while Weber defined class by market situation and life chances. Modern sociologists often classify people into upper, middle and lower classes, or by occupational scales.
Differences between caste and class: caste is ascribed, closed, endogamous and religiously sanctioned; class is achieved, open, not endogamous and secular.
Gender stratification refers to unequal distribution of status, opportunities, responsibilities and power based on socially constructed gender relations.

Sex refers to biological differences between males and females, while gender refers to socially constructed roles, behaviours and identities. Ann Oakley's 'Sex, Gender and Society' (1972) helped popularize this distinction.

Gender stratification is seen in unequal access to education, employment, wages, property, political power and decision-making. Women often bear the 'double burden' of paid work and unpaid domestic work.

Feminist theories explain gender inequality through patriarchy (radical feminism), capitalism and patriarchy together (socialist feminism), or unequal laws and opportunities (liberal feminism). In India, measures such as the Women's Reservation Act, 2023 (the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act), aim to increase women's political representation.
Functional approaches argue that stratification is connected with the allocation of social positions and rewards, though the extent and necessity of inequality remain debated.

Kingsley Davis and Wilbert E. Moore, in 'Some Principles of Stratification' (1945), argued that stratification is universal and necessary because every society must motivate the most talented people to fill the most important positions. Higher rewards are needed to attract people to positions requiring long training and great responsibility.

Melvin Tumin, in 'Some Principles of Stratification: A Critical Analysis' (1953), criticized this theory. He argued that it is difficult to measure the 'functional importance' of positions, that stratification limits the discovery of talent among the poor, that it creates hostility and conflict, and that inherited wealth and power distort the system.
Talcott Parsons also gave a functional view, arguing that stratification reflects the shared values of society.
Marxian analysis locates major inequality in ownership and control of the means of production and emphasizes class conflict.

For Marx, stratification is based on class, which is determined by ownership or non-ownership of the means of production. Inequality is not functional but exploitative, and it benefits the ruling class.
The ruling class also controls ideas, as Marx wrote: 'The ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas'. This ideology hides exploitation and creates false consciousness.
Neo-Marxists such as Erik Olin Wright developed the idea of 'contradictory class locations' to explain the position of managers and professionals in modern capitalism.
Weber treated stratification as multidimensional, involving class, status and party or power rather than economic class alone.

Weber identified three dimensions of stratification: class (economic position in the market, which determines life chances), status (social honour or prestige, expressed in lifestyle) and party (organized groups seeking power, such as political parties).
These three dimensions are related but can vary independently. For example, a priest may have high status but little wealth, while a newly rich businessman may have wealth but less social honour.
Weber's approach is called multidimensional and is useful for analysing modern societies where occupation, education, prestige and political power interact in complex ways.
Social mobility means movement of individuals or groups between social positions. It may be vertical or horizontal and may occur within a lifetime or between generations.

Pitirim Sorokin, in 'Social Mobility' (1927), defined social mobility as 'any transition of an individual or social object or value from one social position to another'. He distinguished horizontal mobility (moving between positions of similar rank, such as changing jobs at the same level) from vertical mobility (moving up or down).

Other types include intragenerational mobility (within a person's lifetime) and intergenerational mobility (between parents and children), as well as individual and group mobility. Structural mobility results from changes in the economy that create new positions.
Factors affecting mobility include education, occupation, migration, urbanization, industrialization, political change, reservation policies and personal ability.
Open systems permit greater movement between positions, while closed systems restrict mobility through hereditary or rigid social boundaries.
In a closed system, such as caste or slavery, status is ascribed at birth and mobility is very limited. In an open system, such as class, status is achieved and mobility is possible.

No society is completely open or completely closed. Even in class societies, family background strongly affects opportunities, while in caste societies some group mobility occurs through Sanskritization, education and politics.
Modern democratic societies aim for equality of opportunity, but structural barriers such as poverty, discrimination and unequal education limit openness.

Social Stratification: Social stratification refers to structured inequality in which individuals and groups are ranked into unequal social positions. It affects access to wealth, power, prestige and opportunities. Characteristics of Stratification: Stratification is social, relatively persistent, hierarchical and connected with unequal rewards and life chances. Its form differs across societies. Caste: Caste is a hereditary form of stratification traditionally associated with hierarchy, endogamy, occupational links and restrictions on social relations. Class: Class is a system of stratification based strongly on economic position and life chances. Class boundaries are generally more open than caste boundaries.

Social stratification is the ranking of individuals and groups into a hierarchy of unequal positions. Tumin's characteristics — social, ancient, universal, diverse and consequential — show that stratification is a basic feature of society that affects life chances.

Caste is a closed, hereditary system based on birth, endogamy, occupational specialization and purity-pollution, as analysed by Ghurye, Dumont and Srinivas. Class is an open system based on economic position, as analysed by Marx (relation to the means of production) and Weber (market situation).

A comparison of caste and class shows differences in openness, basis of membership, religious sanction, endogamy and mobility. In India, caste and class overlap but are increasingly separated in modern economic life.
In conclusion, stratification is universal, but its forms vary. Students should define it, explain its characteristics, and compare caste and class with examples.

Gender and Stratification: Gender stratification refers to unequal distribution of status, opportunities, responsibilities and power based on socially constructed gender relations. Functional Theory of Stratification: Functional approaches argue that stratification is connected with the allocation of social positions and rewards, though the extent and necessity of inequality remain debated. Marxian Theory: Marxian analysis locates major inequality in ownership and control of the means of production and emphasizes class conflict. Weberian Theory: Weber treated stratification as multidimensional, involving class, status and party or power rather than economic class alone.
Gender stratification shows how social roles and power are distributed unequally between men and women. It is explained by feminist theories that highlight patriarchy and unequal opportunities.

Davis and Moore's functional theory claims stratification is necessary for placing talented people in important positions, while Tumin's critique highlights its dysfunctions. Marxian theory sees stratification as rooted in class exploitation and maintained by ideology.
Weber's multidimensional theory distinguishes class, status and party, and helps explain cases where wealth, prestige and power do not coincide.

Each theory provides partial insight: functional theory explains why rewards differ, Marxian theory explains exploitation and conflict, and Weberian theory explains the complexity of modern stratification.

Social Mobility: Social mobility means movement of individuals or groups between social positions. It may be vertical or horizontal and may occur within a lifetime or between generations. Open and Closed Stratification: Open systems permit greater movement between positions, while closed systems restrict mobility through hereditary or rigid social boundaries.

Social mobility is the movement of individuals or groups between positions. Sorokin's distinction between horizontal and vertical mobility, along with intergenerational and intragenerational mobility, provides the basic framework for analysis.
Open systems allow mobility based on achievement, while closed systems restrict it by birth. In practice, all societies combine elements of both.

In India, mobility has increased through education, reservation, urbanization, migration and new occupations. Srinivas's Sanskritization explains group mobility within caste, while education and employment enable individual mobility.
In conclusion, the degree of mobility in a society indicates how open it is and how far it provides equality of opportunity.

blocks.text: This paper continues the study of sociological thought after the classical foundations introduced in Semester V. Students should study each thinker and concept under the exact unit arrangement prescribed in the syllabus.

According to the prescribed syllabus, SOC/MJ/303 has four units: Unit 1 – Herbert Spencer (Theory of Evolution, Theory of Organic Analogy, Types of Society); Unit 2 – A.R. Radcliffe-Brown (Exchange Theory, Social Function, Social Structure); Unit 3 – Bronislaw Malinowski (Theory of Needs, Theory of Culture, Gift Exchange Theory); and Unit 4 – Indian Sociological Thought (Emergence of Indian Sociological Thought, Indology – G.S. Ghurye, Structural Functionalism – M.N. Srinivas, Marxist Sociology – A.R. Desai).

Herbert Spencer (1820-1903), an English thinker, applied the idea of evolution to society. He described evolution as a change from a state of 'indefinite, incoherent homogeneity' to 'definite, coherent heterogeneity' through integration and differentiation. He coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest' in 'Principles of Biology' (1864). His major sociological works are 'The Study of Sociology' (1873) and 'The Principles of Sociology' (1876-1896).

Spencer's organic analogy compared society to a living organism: both grow in size, become more complex in structure as they grow, show differentiation of functions, and have interdependent parts. He also noted differences: the parts of an organism form a concrete whole, while the parts of society are dispersed; consciousness exists in the whole organism, but in society it exists only in individual members.

Spencer classified societies by their degree of composition into simple, compound, doubly compound and trebly compound societies. He also distinguished militant societies (organized for war, with centralized control, compulsory cooperation and subordination of the individual) from industrial societies (organized for production, with decentralized control, voluntary cooperation and individual freedom).

A.R. Radcliffe-Brown (1881-1955), a British social anthropologist, developed structural-functionalism. He studied the Andaman Islanders ('The Andaman Islanders', 1922) and wrote 'Structure and Function in Primitive Society' (1952). He defined social structure as 'the network of actually existing social relations' and social function as the contribution a partial activity makes to the total activity of which it is a part, helping to maintain the structural continuity of society.

Under 'exchange theory', Radcliffe-Brown's study of the Andaman Islanders described how gifts were exchanged at meetings and ceremonies. He argued that the purpose of such exchange was moral rather than economic: it produced friendly feelings and strengthened social bonds between the persons and groups involved.

Bronislaw Malinowski (1884-1942), a Polish-born British anthropologist, is known for his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands. In 'A Scientific Theory of Culture' (1944) he argued that culture exists to satisfy human needs: basic or biological needs (food, reproduction, bodily comfort, safety, movement, growth, health), derived or instrumental needs (economic organization, social control, education, political organization) and integrative needs (knowledge, religion, magic, art). He defined culture as 'the handiwork of man and the medium through which he achieves his ends'.

Malinowski's study of the Kula ring in 'Argonauts of the Western Pacific' (1922) is the classic example of gift exchange. In the Kula, red shell necklaces (soulava) moved clockwise and white shell armbands (mwali) moved anticlockwise around a ring of islands. The objects were not kept permanently but passed on, and their exchange created lasting partnerships, prestige and social ties. Marcel Mauss later analysed such exchange in 'The Gift' (1925), stressing the obligations to give, to receive and to reciprocate.

Indian sociology emerged when the University of Bombay set up a department of Sociology in 1919 under Patrick Geddes, followed by the University of Lucknow in 1921 with Radhakamal Mukerjee and later D.P. Mukerji. G.S. Ghurye, who headed the Bombay department, represented the Indological approach, which studies Indian society through classical texts; his works include 'Caste and Race in India' (1932) and 'The Scheduled Tribes'.

M.N. Srinivas represented the structural-functional approach, based on fieldwork ('the field view' rather than 'the book view'). He introduced Sanskritization, Westernization, dominant caste and vote bank. A.R. Desai represented Marxist sociology; in 'Social Background of Indian Nationalism' (1948) he explained the rise of nationalism through the economic and class changes brought by colonial capitalism, and he also wrote on rural sociology and peasant struggles.
