blocks.text: Sociological Thought – II: This paper continues the study of sociological thought after the classical foundations introduced in Semester V. Students should study each thinker and concept under the exact unit arrangement prescribed in the syllabus.

Herbert Spencer's sociology is built on the idea of evolution. Society, like nature, evolves from simple to complex through integration (coming together of parts) and differentiation (specialization of parts). This general law applies to the inorganic, organic and super-organic (social) worlds.

Spencer's organic analogy states that society is like an organism. Both grow, both become structurally more complex as they grow, both show a division of functions among parts, and in both the parts are interdependent; the failure of one part affects the whole. Spencer compared the sustaining system of society (industry) to the alimentary system, the distributing system (transport and trade) to the circulatory system, and the regulating system (government) to the nervous system. He accepted that the analogy is not perfect because consciousness in society lies only in individuals.

Spencer classified societies by composition (simple, compound, doubly compound, trebly compound) and by type of organization (militant and industrial). Militant societies emphasize war, centralized authority and compulsory cooperation, while industrial societies emphasize peaceful production, voluntary cooperation and individual liberty. He believed societies would move towards the industrial type. Critics argue that his evolutionism was too linear and that his 'social Darwinism' was used to justify inequality and colonialism.

A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, influenced by Durkheim, treated social anthropology as a 'natural science of society'. Social structure is the arrangement of persons in institutionally defined relationships, such as kinship, while structural form is the general pattern that persists even as individuals change. Social function is the contribution of an institution, such as a ritual or kinship rule, to the maintenance of the social structure. In his Andaman study, he showed how ceremonies and the exchange of gifts expressed and strengthened social sentiments and solidarity. He also analysed joking and avoidance relationships as ways of managing potential conflict in kinship.

Bronislaw Malinowski developed a functionalism based on individual needs rather than on the structure of society. His theory of needs holds that culture responds to basic biological needs, which give rise to derived needs and integrative needs; every cultural institution exists to satisfy one or more needs. For example, the family satisfies reproduction and child care, and magic reduces anxiety in uncertain activities such as deep-sea fishing.

Malinowski's theory of culture treats culture as an instrumental reality, an integrated whole of institutions, each with a charter, personnel, norms, material apparatus, activities and function. His study of the Kula ring showed that exchange in the Trobriand Islands was not merely economic but created alliances, prestige, obligations and trust between partners across islands. Gift exchange was therefore a 'total social phenomenon' (as Mauss later called it) linking economic, social, religious and political life.

Indian sociological thought emerged in the early twentieth century, with departments established at Bombay (1919) and Lucknow (1921). The early phase was shaped by Indology, the study of Indian society through Sanskrit texts and history. G.S. Ghurye, the leading Indologist, analysed caste through six features (segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, restriction on occupation, endogamy), studied tribes as 'backward Hindus', and wrote on culture, sadhus and urbanization.

M.N. Srinivas brought the structural-functional approach and intensive fieldwork to Indian sociology through his studies of the Coorgs (1952) and Rampura. His concepts of Sanskritization, Westernization, dominant caste and vote bank remain central to the study of Indian social change.

A.R. Desai, a Marxist sociologist, used historical materialism to analyse Indian society. In 'Social Background of Indian Nationalism' (1948) he argued that colonial rule transformed the Indian economy and created new classes, such as the industrial bourgeoisie, the working class and the educated middle class, which gave rise to nationalism. He criticized the development path of independent India as capitalist and studied peasant and agrarian struggles.

In conclusion, this paper shows how evolutionary, structural-functional and Marxist approaches developed in Western thought and how Indian sociologists adapted these approaches through Indology, fieldwork and Marxist analysis to understand Indian society.
Social research is the systematic investigation of social phenomena using organized methods of inquiry. It aims to describe, explain and understand social relationships and processes.

P.V. Young defined social research as 'a scientific undertaking which, by means of logical and systematized techniques, aims to discover new facts or verify old facts, analyse their sequences, interrelationships and causal explanations'.

The aims of social research include discovering new facts, verifying existing knowledge, explaining social phenomena, developing theories, predicting social trends and helping solve social problems through planning and policy.

The syllabus lists three approaches: quantitative (numbers and statistics), qualitative (meanings and context) and mixed methods (combining both). The steps in scientific research are selection and formulation of the problem, review of literature, formulation of hypotheses, research design, sampling, data collection, analysis, interpretation and report writing.
The scientific method involves systematic observation, clear concepts, evidence, logical analysis and conclusions that can be examined critically.
The characteristics of scientific research include objectivity, verifiability, generality, predictability, systematic procedure, ethical neutrality and the use of concepts and theory.
Scientific research uses both induction (from particular observations to general conclusions) and deduction (from theory to specific predictions to be tested).

Applying the scientific method to society is difficult because human behaviour is complex and changing, people may alter their behaviour when observed, and the researcher's own values may affect the study.
A research problem is a clearly defined issue or question selected for systematic investigation. A good problem should be specific, researchable and sociologically relevant.

Sources of research problems include personal experience, existing theory, review of literature, current social problems and policy needs. A good problem should be clear, specific, significant, feasible and ethically acceptable.
Formulating the problem involves selecting a broad area, narrowing it down, reviewing literature, identifying gaps and stating specific research questions or objectives.
A hypothesis is a tentative and testable statement about a relationship between variables or social phenomena.

Goode and Hatt defined a hypothesis as 'a proposition which can be put to test to determine its validity'. It states an expected relationship between an independent variable (the presumed cause) and a dependent variable (the effect).

A good hypothesis is clear, specific, testable, related to available techniques and connected with theory. A null hypothesis states that there is no relationship, while an alternative hypothesis states that a relationship exists.
A research design is the overall plan that connects the research problem, data collection and analysis. It helps ensure that evidence is collected in an organized manner.

The syllabus also lists the types of research: basic (pure) research, which aims to add to knowledge; applied research, which aims to solve practical problems; action research, survey research and ethnography.

Action research, associated with the psychologist Kurt Lewin (1946), is research carried out together with the people concerned in order to solve a practical problem and bring about change. It follows a cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting, and is used in education, community development and organizations.
Research designs may be exploratory, descriptive, diagnostic or experimental. A good research design is flexible, efficient, economical, appropriate to the problem and minimizes bias.
Quantitative research uses numerical data and measurement to identify patterns, relationships or distributions.
Quantitative research is based on positivism and uses surveys, structured questionnaires, experiments and statistical analysis. It allows generalization from large samples and testing of hypotheses.
Its limitations include difficulty in capturing meanings, feelings and context. Examples include the Census and the National Family Health Survey.
Qualitative research emphasizes meanings, experiences and social contexts, often using interviews, observation and textual material.

Qualitative research uses participant observation, in-depth interviews, focus groups, case studies, life histories and content analysis. It provides depth and understanding of meanings but usually uses small samples.

Ethnography, listed in the syllabus, is the detailed study of a community or group through long-term fieldwork and participant observation, aiming to understand social life from the participants' point of view. Malinowski's Trobriand study and Srinivas's Rampura study are classic examples.

Mixed methods research combines quantitative and qualitative methods, for example a survey followed by in-depth interviews, so that the strengths of one approach make up for the weaknesses of the other.
Primary data are collected directly by the researcher for the study, while secondary data already exist in documents, records, reports or earlier research.

Primary data are original data collected by the researcher through observation, interviews, questionnaires, schedules and case studies. Secondary data come from existing sources such as census reports, government publications, NSSO and NFHS reports, books, journals, newspapers, diaries and archives.
Primary data are specific to the study but costly and time-consuming. Secondary data are cheaper and quicker but must be checked for reliability, suitability and adequacy.
A survey collects standardized information from respondents, commonly through questionnaires or schedules.

Survey research collects standardized information from a large number of respondents using questionnaires or interview schedules. Surveys may be cross-sectional (at one point in time) or longitudinal (repeated over time).

A questionnaire is filled in by the respondent and is suitable for literate respondents; an interview schedule is filled in by the researcher who asks the questions face to face and is useful when respondents are illiterate. A pilot study helps test the tool before the main survey.
An interview collects information through direct questioning and interaction between researcher and respondent.
Interviews may be structured (fixed questions in a fixed order), unstructured (flexible conversation), semi-structured, focused or group interviews.

Advantages include depth of information, flexibility and use with illiterate respondents; disadvantages include interviewer bias, cost and the possibility of socially desirable answers. Good interviewing requires rapport, careful listening and accurate recording.

A case study, also listed in the syllabus, is an intensive study of a single unit, such as a person, family, institution, community or event, in its full context. Frederic Le Play's studies of working-class families in nineteenth-century Europe are often cited as early examples.
Observation involves systematic watching and recording of behaviour, interaction or social settings.
Observation may be participant (the researcher takes part in the life of the group) or non-participant, and structured (using a fixed schedule) or unstructured.

William Foote Whyte's 'Street Corner Society' (1943) is a famous example of participant observation. Observation gives direct and natural data but can be affected by observer bias and by the 'Hawthorne effect', when people change their behaviour because they know they are being observed.
Sampling is the selection of a smaller group from a larger population for study. Appropriate sampling helps make research manageable and relevant.

Probability sampling, in which every unit has a known chance of selection, includes simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster sampling. Non-probability sampling includes convenience, purposive, quota and snowball sampling.
A good sample is representative of the population, adequate in size and drawn from an accurate sampling frame.

The syllabus also lists problems of objectivity. Objectivity means studying facts as they are, without personal bias. In social research, objectivity is difficult because the researcher is part of society and holds values, respondents may hide information, and social facts are complex. Max Weber argued for 'value-neutrality' in research while accepting that values influence the choice of topic. Objectivity can be improved through standardized tools, careful sampling, team research, cross-checking data and honest reporting.

Social Research: Social research is the systematic investigation of social phenomena using organized methods of inquiry. It aims to describe, explain and understand social relationships and processes. Scientific Method: The scientific method involves systematic observation, clear concepts, evidence, logical analysis and conclusions that can be examined critically. Research Problem: A research problem is a clearly defined issue or question selected for systematic investigation. A good problem should be specific, researchable and sociologically relevant. Hypothesis: A hypothesis is a tentative and testable statement about a relationship between variables or social phenomena.

Unit I of SOC/MJ/304 covers the meaning and aims of social research, the characteristics of scientific research, the qualitative, quantitative and mixed approaches, and the steps in scientific research.
Social research is the systematic, scientific study of social life. Its aims are to discover and verify facts, explain relationships, build theory and help solve social problems.
Scientific research is objective, verifiable, systematic, general and predictive. It begins with a clear research problem and usually a hypothesis that guides data collection.
In conclusion, social research applies the scientific method to society, while recognizing the special difficulties of studying human behaviour.

Research Design: A research design is the overall plan that connects the research problem, data collection and analysis. It helps ensure that evidence is collected in an organized manner. Quantitative Research: Quantitative research uses numerical data and measurement to identify patterns, relationships or distributions. Qualitative Research: Qualitative research emphasizes meanings, experiences and social contexts, often using interviews, observation and textual material. Primary and Secondary Data: Primary data are collected directly by the researcher for the study, while secondary data already exist in documents, records, reports or earlier research.

Unit II covers the types of research: basic research adds to knowledge, applied research solves practical problems, action research involves participants in solving problems and bringing change, survey research collects standardized data from large numbers, and ethnography studies a community in depth through fieldwork.

Unit III covers research design and sampling. Research design is the blueprint of a study and may be exploratory, descriptive, diagnostic or experimental. Sampling design involves defining the population, preparing a sampling frame and choosing probability or non-probability methods.
Problems of objectivity arise from the researcher's values, respondents' reactions and the complexity of social facts, and can be reduced through careful methods.
In conclusion, a good research design and an appropriate sample are essential for reliable and valid findings.

Survey: A survey collects standardized information from respondents, commonly through questionnaires or schedules. Interview: An interview collects information through direct questioning and interaction between researcher and respondent. Observation: Observation involves systematic watching and recording of behaviour, interaction or social settings. Sampling: Sampling is the selection of a smaller group from a larger population for study. Appropriate sampling helps make research manageable and relevant.
Unit IV covers techniques of data collection: primary and secondary data, observation, questionnaires and interview schedules, and the case study.

Observation provides first-hand data on behaviour in natural settings. Questionnaires and schedules collect standardized information, the questionnaire being filled in by the respondent and the schedule by the investigator. Interviews give depth and flexibility.
The case study method examines a single unit intensively and is useful for understanding processes and context, though its findings may not be easy to generalize.
In conclusion, researchers usually combine several techniques, and the choice depends on the research problem, the population, available resources and ethical considerations.
Urban Sociology studies cities, urban social relationships, institutions, population patterns and processes of urban change.
According to the syllabus, Unit I of SOC/MJ/305 covers the development and scope of urban sociology, its significance, urbanism and rurbanization (rural-urban convergence).

Urban sociology developed especially through the Chicago School in the 1920s and 1930s, when Robert E. Park, Ernest W. Burgess, Roderick McKenzie and Louis Wirth studied the city as a 'social laboratory'. Its scope includes urban growth, urban social structure, family, neighbourhoods, migration, slums, urban problems, urban planning and governance.

Its significance lies in helping to understand and plan cities, which now hold more than half of the world's population, and in addressing urban problems such as housing, poverty, crime and pollution.
Urbanization is the growth of urban population and expansion of urban ways of life. It is closely connected with industrialization, migration and economic transformation.
Kingsley Davis defined urbanization as the process of moving from a dispersed to a more concentrated pattern of settlement. In India, Census 2011 recorded 31.1 per cent of the population as urban.

Factors of urbanization include industrialization, migration from villages, the growth of trade and services, transport and communication, education and administrative centres. Mizoram is one of the most urbanized states in India, with about 52 per cent of its population urban in 2011, mainly in Aizawl.

Types of cities can be classified by function (administrative, industrial, commercial, port, educational, religious, hill station) or by size (town, city, metropolis, megalopolis). Gideon Sjoberg distinguished the 'pre-industrial city' from the 'industrial city', and Lewis Mumford described stages of city growth from 'eopolis' and 'polis' to 'metropolis', 'megalopolis', 'tyrannopolis' and 'nekropolis'.
Urbanism refers to social patterns and ways of life associated with urban settings, including greater occupational specialization, mobility and impersonal relations.

Louis Wirth, in 'Urbanism as a Way of Life' (1938), defined the city as 'a relatively large, dense and permanent settlement of socially heterogeneous individuals' and argued that size, density and heterogeneity produce a distinctive urban way of life, marked by secondary relations, anonymity, specialization and formal social control.
Georg Simmel, in 'The Metropolis and Mental Life' (1903), described the 'blase attitude' of city dwellers. Herbert Gans later showed that many city dwellers live in close-knit 'urban villages'.

Rurbanization refers to the convergence of rural and urban ways of life, where villages acquire urban facilities and lifestyles while keeping rural features. The term 'rurban' was used by C.J. Galpin in 1918. In India, the Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (2016) aims to develop clusters of villages with urban amenities.
Cities and villages are connected through migration, markets, employment, transport, education, communication and flows of goods and resources.

Rural-urban linkages include migration and remittances, markets for agricultural and manufactured goods, commuting, access to education and health services, communication and the spread of urban values to villages.
Many migrants maintain ties with their villages, and the return of migrant workers during the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020 showed how closely villages and cities are linked.
Urban social structure includes differentiated occupations, classes, neighbourhoods, associations and diverse cultural groups.
Unit III of the syllabus covers urban social structure: urban family and kinship, urban culture, urban neighbourhood and voluntary associations.

Urban families tend to be smaller and nuclear, with more equal relations between husband and wife and more employed women, but kinship ties continue through visits, help in crises, ceremonies and phone or online contact. Urban culture is diverse, secular, individualistic and influenced by mass media and consumerism.

An urban neighbourhood is a residential area where people share facilities and some social interaction, though ties are usually weaker than in villages. Voluntary associations, such as residents' welfare associations, clubs, trade unions, professional bodies and religious groups, help people form social networks in the city. In Aizawl, localities have Local Councils and branches of the YMA, MHIP and churches that maintain strong community life.
Migration is movement of people from one place to another for work, education, family or other reasons. Rural-to-urban migration is a major factor in city growth.
Migration may be internal or international, rural-to-urban, rural-to-rural, urban-to-urban or urban-to-rural, and seasonal, temporary or permanent.

Everett Lee's push-pull theory explains migration through push factors (poverty, unemployment, conflict, disasters), pull factors (jobs, education, services) and intervening obstacles such as distance and cost.
Rapid urban growth may produce housing shortages, congestion, inadequate services, unemployment, inequality, pollution and other problems.
Urban problems include housing shortages, slums, traffic congestion, pollution, solid waste, water scarcity, unemployment, the informal economy, crime and inequality.
In hill cities such as Aizawl, specific problems include landslides, traffic on narrow roads, water supply and limited flat land.
Slums are densely settled urban areas commonly characterized by inadequate housing, infrastructure and basic services. Their growth is connected with poverty, migration and unequal urban development.
Census 2011 counted about 6.5 crore people living in slums in India. Causes include migration, poverty, lack of affordable housing and unplanned growth.
Programmes include the Rajiv Awas Yojana and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (2015), which promotes slum redevelopment and affordable housing.
Urban planning is the organized management of land use, housing, transport, infrastructure and public services to improve urban life.
Unit IV of the syllabus covers urban development: the role of the municipality, urban development programmes, urban planning and urban social change.

The 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to urban local bodies: municipal corporations for large cities, municipal councils for smaller cities and nagar panchayats for areas in transition from rural to urban. The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 functions, including urban planning, water supply, public health, sanitation, slum improvement and poverty alleviation. Aizawl has a Municipal Corporation with elected councillors.

Urban development programmes include JNNURM (2005), the Smart Cities Mission (2015), AMRUT (2015), PMAY-Urban (2015) and the Swachh Bharat Mission – Urban (2014). Urban social change includes the growth of the middle class, nuclear families, women's employment, new lifestyles and consumer culture, along with new problems of inequality and isolation.

Unit I: Urban sociology developed through the Chicago School and studies cities, urban life and urban problems. Its significance lies in understanding and planning cities. Urbanism, as described by Wirth and Simmel, is the distinctive urban way of life. Rurbanization is the convergence of rural and urban life, seen in villages acquiring urban amenities.

Unit II: Theories of urbanization explain the spatial growth of cities. Burgess's concentric zone theory (1925) describes rings around the central business district: the zone in transition, the zone of workingmen's homes, the residential zone and the commuter zone. Homer Hoyt's sector theory (1939) argues that cities grow in sectors along transport routes. Harris and Ullman's multiple-nuclei theory (1945) argues that cities develop around several centres.

The ecological theory of the Chicago School, developed by Park, Burgess and McKenzie, views the city as an environment where groups compete for space, as in nature. Ecological processes include concentration, centralization, segregation, invasion and succession.

In conclusion, students should explain each theory with a simple diagram where possible, discuss factors of urbanization and types of cities, and apply them to Indian cities, which often show a mixture of patterns.

Social conflict arises when individuals or groups pursue incompatible interests, values, resources or power. Conflict may produce disruption but can also contribute to social change.
According to the syllabus, Unit I of SOC/MJ/306 covers the characteristics, causes, stages and types of social conflict.

Characteristics of conflict: it is universal, conscious, personal or group-based, intermittent rather than continuous, and may be violent or non-violent. Causes include scarcity of resources, unequal distribution of power and wealth, differences in values and culture, rapid social change, and competition between groups.

Stages of conflict are often described as latent conflict (hidden tension), perceived conflict, felt conflict, manifest conflict (open struggle) and conflict aftermath (resolution or renewed conflict). Types include personal, class, caste, racial, ethnic, communal, political and international conflict.

Theorists include Karl Marx (class conflict), Ralf Dahrendorf ('Class and Class Conflict in Industrial Society', 1959, conflict over authority), Lewis Coser ('The Functions of Social Conflict', 1956) and Randall Collins ('Conflict Sociology', 1975).
A social movement is organized collective action aimed at promoting, resisting or reversing social change.

Herbert Blumer described social movements as 'collective enterprises to establish a new order of life'. Paul Wilkinson defined a social movement as 'a deliberate collective endeavour to promote change in any direction and by any means'.
Social movements differ from crowds and riots because they are organized, sustained and goal-oriented.
Social movements involve collective participation, shared objectives, some degree of organization and sustained action beyond isolated individual behaviour.
Characteristics include collective action, a shared goal of change, an ideology, organization, leadership, collective identity and sustained activity.

The formation of a movement usually passes through stages: emergence (social unrest), coalescence (organization and leadership), bureaucratization (formal organization), and decline through success, repression, co-optation or failure.
Movements may seek reform within existing institutions, radical transformation, protection of identities or resistance to unwanted change.

David Aberle classified movements as alternative, redemptive, reformative and transformative. Other types include reform, revolutionary, resistance, identity and new social movements (concerned with environment, gender, peace and human rights).

Theories of social movements listed in the syllabus can be explained as follows: relative deprivation theory (Ted Gurr, 'Why Men Rebel', 1970) holds that movements arise when people feel deprived compared with their expectations; structural strain theory (Neil Smelser, 'Theory of Collective Behaviour', 1962) lists six conditions: structural conduciveness, structural strain, generalized belief, precipitating factors, mobilization and the operation of social control; resource mobilization theory (McCarthy and Zald) emphasizes resources and organization; and new social movement theory (Alain Touraine, Alberto Melucci) emphasizes identity and culture.
Leadership provides direction and mobilization, while organization helps coordinate participants, resources and strategies.
Unit III of the syllabus covers three movements in modern India: the Santhal Movement, the Naxalbari Movement and the Mizo National Front.

The Santhal Hul (rebellion) of 1855-56 was led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu in the Damin-i-koh region of the Rajmahal hills. The Santhals rose against zamindars, moneylenders and traders (whom they called 'dikus') and against colonial officials who supported them. The rebellion was suppressed, but the British created the separate Santhal Parganas district, and the movement became a symbol of tribal resistance.

The Naxalbari Movement began in 1967 in the Naxalbari area of Darjeeling district in West Bengal, when peasants and tribal sharecroppers, led by Charu Majumdar, Kanu Sanyal and Jangal Santhal, seized land from landlords. The Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) was formed in 1969. The term 'Naxalite' comes from this movement, which inspired armed agrarian struggles in several states.
Ideology gives a movement a framework for interpreting problems, defining goals and justifying collective action.

The Mizo National Front (MNF) movement grew out of the Mautam famine of 1959, caused by bamboo flowering and a rat explosion, and the inadequate relief response. The Mizo National Famine Front, formed for relief work, became the Mizo National Front in 1961 under Laldenga, demanding independence for the Mizo people.

The MNF launched an armed uprising in March 1966, and the Lushai Hills experienced two decades of insurgency, military operations and the grouping of villages. Mizoram became a Union Territory in 1972. After long negotiations, the Mizo Peace Accord was signed on 30 June 1986, and Mizoram became a full state in February 1987, with Laldenga as Chief Minister.

Sociologically, the MNF movement shows how ethnic identity, economic grievance, religion (Christianity) and a sense of neglect can produce a movement for self-determination, and how democratic accommodation can bring lasting peace. Mizoram is often cited as one of the most successful examples of conflict resolution in India.
Collective identity is the sense of shared belonging that connects participants and strengthens solidarity within a movement.
Unit IV of the syllabus covers post-independence women's movements and backward classes movements.

Post-independence women's movements gained strength in the 1970s after the report 'Towards Equality' (1974) of the Committee on the Status of Women in India showed continuing inequality. Major issues included dowry deaths, rape (the Mathura case led to amendments in rape law in 1983), domestic violence, personal law (the Shah Bano case, 1985), political representation, and violence against women (protests after the Delhi gang rape of 2012 led to the Criminal Law Amendment of 2013).

Types of women's movements include liberal (legal reform and equal rights), socialist and Marxist (linking gender with class), radical (challenging patriarchy), grassroots movements such as the anti-arrack movement in Andhra Pradesh, and women's participation in environmental movements such as Chipko. In Mizoram, the Mizo Hmeichhe Insuihkhawm Pawl (MHIP), formed in 1974, has worked on women's rights, including property and inheritance rights.
Movements can influence laws, policies, institutions, public opinion and cultural values. Their effects may be direct or gradual.

Backward classes movements sought dignity, equality and a share in education, jobs and power. Examples include Jyotirao Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) in Maharashtra, the SNDP Yogam (1903) inspired by Sree Narayana Guru in Kerala, E.V. Ramasamy Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (1925) in Tamil Nadu, B.R. Ambedkar's movements for Dalit rights, the Dalit Panthers (1972), and the mobilization around the Mandal Commission recommendations (1990).

M.S.A. Rao classified backward classes movements by their aims and methods, distinguishing reformist movements, which sought change within the system, from transformative movements, which challenged the caste hierarchy itself. The nature of these movements has moved from social reform and Sanskritization towards political mobilization and assertion of identity.

Movements can influence laws, policies, institutions and culture, as shown by the Right to Information Act (2005), forest rights legislation, reservation policies and the creation of new states such as Mizoram.
